issues.legal_issue: The will’s intended ultimate succession was clear despite its omission of words expressly addressing succession after the life tenant’s death.
material_facts: The will gave the testator’s wife a life interest in his estate and expressly provided that his son would take the estate if his wife died before him.
The will stated that the testator’s daughter-in-law and granddaughters would have no right or share in his estate.
The will directed that charitable acts be continued by the son after the wife’s death.
The will did not expressly state who would take the estate if the wife survived the testator and later died.
The dispute concerned a sum deposited in banks, and the son claimed it under the will.
issues.conclusion: The son alone was entitled to succeed to the estate after the wife’s death; the necessary omitted words could be read into the will.
issues.legal_principle: A court may supply words omitted from a will where it is clear from the will as a whole both that the testator did not completely express his meaning and what words were omitted, and the intended meaning is established by compelling probability rather than speculation. The Court relied on William Abbott v. Eliza Middleton, Eden v. Wilson, Re Smith, Re Cory, Re Riley’s Will Trusts, and the statement of the principle in Jarman on Wills, 8th edition, page 592.

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The proceeding concerns the construction of a testator’s will.
predicates.clear_ultimate_beneficiary_intent: The will, read as a whole, identifies the intended ultimate recipient of the estate through its provisions about the life tenant, alternative succession, excluded relatives, or duties after the life tenant’s death.
predicates.omitted_succession_words_identifiable: The will leaves out words addressing a succession circumstance, but the words needed to express the testator’s intention are ascertainable from the will as a whole.

issues.definition: When a will-construction dispute shows a clear ultimate beneficiary and identifiable omitted succession words, the necessary words are supplied to effectuate the will.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not interfere with an appellate court’s discretionary refusal to receive additional evidence when the application is very belated.
material_facts: An application to receive additional evidence was made in the High Court many years after the suit began and years after the appeal was filed.
The principal evidence sought was an alleged letter to a bank nominating a person entitled to the deposited funds.
The letter was not attached to the application; the applicant asked the High Court to summon it from the bank.
The High Court refused the application, and the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with that discretionary decision.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s discretionary refusal to receive the additional evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court’s exercise of discretion to refuse additional evidence where the application is made very late.

predicates.appellate_additional_evidence_applicatio: A party seeks to introduce additional evidence in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.application_very_belated: The application to introduce the evidence is made many years after the suit began and after a substantial period has passed since the appeal was filed.

issues.definition: When a party makes a very belated application for additional evidence in an appellate proceeding, the refusal to receive it is left undisturbed.
